brief_context: Origin of the Panel of Technical Advisers.
brief_extract:
Amenities—Technical Skill—
Architectural Excellence
The Scottish people cherish the
great heritage of beauty gifted to
them by nature, and Parliament
was equally jealous in guarding
it; to ensure that the Board's
water-power schemes will not un-
duly conflict with amenity, the
Secretary of State appointed an
Amenity Committee. A Panel of
Technical Advisers, consisting of
the most eminent civil, mechan-
ical and electrical engineers in
Great Britain, was appointed,
having the collaboration of a
Panel of three eminently skilled
architects. Fisheries Committee
The Fisheries Committee was
also appointed, to ensure that
the stock of salmon and sea-trout
in Scottish rivers is preserved.

BOOKS
" They Made Invasion Possible " by Peggy Scott (Hutchinson 15/-) tells in a warm human way of all those duties, great and small, re- quiring skill, physical effort, courage and a constantly high morale, gladly and gallantly undertaken by the women of Britain, who had their first general reward in the successful invasion of Europe in 1944. Official facts are clothed by the insight into women's lives and work gained by Miss Scott in her extensive tours, and a truer picture is thus given of Britain's women at war from her recorded conversations with Service-women, Land Girls, Industrial and Civil Defence workers.

brief_context: The primary country visited during a month's tour.
brief_extract:
THE ELECTRICAL AGE. APRIL, 1945

SCANDINAVIAN MID-WINTER

A VISIT made by air to a neutral country in a Scandinavian mid-winter leaves so many impressions that it is difficult to select from the many the few that will best give a picture of a month's tour of Sweden and brief 36-hour trip to Finland. Snow and Transport
First, there is the snow, which makes more beautiful a country already lovely in natural scenery and architecture, but when it is realised that the snow was the deepest in Sweden for seven years you can imagine what air and train travel were like!

brief_context: City where the author visited the Art Museum.
brief_extract:
Since visiting Sweden for the World Power Conference the years of war have tended to erase from one's mind the remembrance of another country and its social customs, but it was refreshing to rediscover them. Architecture and the Arts
Time did not permit a leisured appreciation of Sweden's fine architecture and other artistic and cultural pursuits, but in Gothenburg I was impressed by the wonderful Square with its grouping of the lovely Art Museum, new Municipal Theatre and Concert Hall. THE EDITOR.

Audiences included business and professional women, Trades Union officials, diplomatic representatives from several countries, electrical engineers, Anglo-Swedish societies, architects and housing officials, University lecturers from the Home Economics and Nutrition Departments.

brief_extract:
W. DALE, General Manager and Secretary,
British Electrical Development Association

AT any time prospecting is
vastly more interesting than
retrospecting: at a time when
Bomber Command subscribes to
the point of view that the
mighty atom has transformed
battleships and Lancasters into
the dodo and when old-estab-
lished gentlemen in Fleet Street
openly recommend the disposal
of our orthodox history books, it
does indeed demand exceptional
effort to tempt anyone to re-
tread old paths. Nevertheless, at
this time, when the British Elec-
trical Development Association
is privileged to honour its sister
Association's coming of age in
an essentially practical manner it
is not inappropriate that we
should pause for a brief space to
survey broadly the influence of
twenty-one years of electrical
development in the domestic
sphere — more especially for the
reason that the Association's
celebrations happily coincide
with an unparalleled phase in
scientific achievement and at a
time when the electrical answer
to quo vadis was never more
positive and assured.

knows how to use electricity
efficiently and economically—to-
morrow, she will know even

work are cumulative and our
programme is increasing. Educational Activities
These twenty-one years have
witnessed the progressive estab-
lishment of electrical housecraft
and demonstration centres — pri-
marily for service to the house-
wife—in virtually every town in
the Kingdom. Many hundreds of
skilled and trained women have
been appointed to give practical
help and advice, not only at
their showroom bases and in
women’s organisations, but right
in the homes of the people.

We live with a generation
which takes innovation very much
for granted : for example, at
least seven to eight million
families in Great Britain can
now switch on the electric light
in their own homes where they
could not do so twenty-one years
ago. Although so short an inter-
val has elapsed as to bring the
period well within our purview,
few people can scarcely recall
what it really meant to be with-
out this clean, constant and in-
stantaneous service.

CONTRASTS

A Journey to the Middle East

By CAROLINE HASLETT

LEAVING England on June 27th to fly to the Middle East at the request of the Central Advisory Council for Education in H.M. Forces, on July 29th I was back home, having travelled by air, by road, by rail, speaking to Service men and women in desert camps and the big cities of Egypt, Palestine and the Suez Canal Zone, visiting Cairo, Jerusalem, Haifa, Tel Aviv, Alexandria, Ismailia. brief_context: Mentioned for its Old City and hallowed places.
brief_extract:
I saw Arab villages, and visited the Jewish collective settlements,
whose achievements are great both in cultivation of the soil and
of a communal way of living, where men and women work to-
gether on an equal footing and where a greater measure of inde-
pendence is permitted by the general conviction of the priority
of the common good. The wonders of Tutankhamen's Tomb in Cairo; the Old City
wtihin the Walls of Jerusalem, with its hallowed places of many
faiths; an open-air concert on the Mount of Olives overlooking
the Jordan Valley, the Dead Sea and the Moab Hills; a motor
ride along the Nile and through the uncanny Dead City, with its
mile of deserted houses and innumerable tombstones; and
finally the return air journey over El Alamein, Tobruk, Ben-
ghazi and the other recently famous battlefields of North
Africa, to arrive in England after 21 hours in the air—these
are the geographical highlights of a visit of contrasted scenes,
persons and circumstances. A DEBT TO RADAR

THE preservation of Britain owes much to Radar (the
term now used for Radiolocation), and the victorious United Nations
owe an immeasurable debt to Great Britain and her scientists.
